overview: This file traces the organization, regulation, political influence, and growing state control of the Japanese press from 1930 to 1934. Its centerpiece is a comprehensive U.S. Embassy survey of newspaper history, circulation, ownership, finances, ethics, management, and legal restrictions, accompanied by an English translation of Japan’s 1909 Press Law. Subsequent reports document shifts in newspaper ownership and political affiliation amid international crisis and rising militarism, concealed Foreign Office financial control of the Japan Times and Mail, and plans to consolidate Japan’s leading news agencies into a centralized instrument of government influence and propaganda.
interest: The file is especially useful because it combines a broad structural account of Japan’s newspaper industry with confidential reporting on particular mechanisms of state influence. It allows historians to compare the press system in 1930 with its increasingly politicized and centralized form during the Manchurian and diplomatic crises of the early 1930s. The evidence of concealed Foreign Office financing and concern over a government-controlled news-agency merger offers unusually concrete insight into how information management and propaganda developed before Japan’s later wartime press controls.
